I force myself to think only positive thoughts
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: This strategy is socially anxious/interpersonal in content and is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by war-zone danger cues, hypervigilant threat monitoring, and trauma-memory reactivation. The other strategies and threat/memory items coherently reflect trauma-related safety management, but rehearsing conversations before any interaction targets a different problem domain that is not represented elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, or Memory. Given the formulation, maladaptive strategies should plausibly feed back into triggers/threat/memory; this item does not connect well to those active nodes.

vignette:
Ethan is a 29-year-old single man who works as a jeweler, spending long hours at a bench under bright task lights, repairing clasps, resetting stones, and speaking with customers across glass cases that display small expensive objects. Before seeking help, he had spent months telling himself that what happened to him overseas “could have been worse,” a phrase he returned to so often it had become almost automatic. He had gone to a war zone as a relief worker and was assigned to a distribution site where families gathered for food, water, and basic supplies. The moment that remains fixed for him occurred during what had seemed like a routine aid handout. There had been a dense crowd, adults pressing forward, children crying nearby, and Ethan trying to focus on who needed what. Then the atmosphere shifted. He remembers becoming aware, all at once, that people were shouting in different directions and that his own heart was pounding so hard he could feel it in his throat. Someone grabbed him unexpectedly from behind to pull him down and move him, and in the same instant he registered the crying of children cutting through the noise around him. What stayed with him was not a single neat sequence so much as the terrible conviction that ordinary humanitarian work had become a place where he could be hurt or killed without warning.

In the weeks after he returned to the United States, Ethan tried to carry on as if he had simply come back from difficult fieldwork. He did not want to sound dramatic, and he was quick to tell himself that other people had lost far more than he had. If the memory pressed close, he forced himself toward upbeat thoughts, insisting that he was lucky, that he should focus on the good, that dwelling on anything dark would only make him weak or ungrateful. Outwardly this made him seem composed. Internally, the event remained alarmingly close. He found that something in his surroundings could bring the whole experience back with no warning at all. A child crying in a grocery store could jolt him into the same flood of alarm before he had even consciously placed the sound. Sometimes he would not get an image at all; instead the feeling arrived first and whole, a surge of dread and bodily urgency so strong that he felt he was back there emotionally even if he could not picture the scene. When the memory did come in full, it felt more vivid and real than whatever was in front of him.

His work as a jeweler gave these reactions frequent places to land. The store required attentiveness to security, and Ethan found himself taking that far beyond what others considered normal. He noticed potential weapons or dangerous objects in every environment: a heavy metal hole punch on a coworker’s desk, a letter opener near the register, a customer’s umbrella with a pointed tip, the tools on his own bench. He chose seats with his back to the wall in the break room and positioned himself carefully on the sales floor so he could see the entrance and most of the room at once. If someone came up beside him while he was bent over a repair and touched his shoulder unexpectedly, his body reacted before he could think, with a violent jolt of fear and a pounding heart that felt immediately meaningful to him, as if his own body were sounding an alarm that danger was already underway. When colleagues or friends told him, reasonably, that he was safe here, he found the reassurance impossible to take in. Safety, to him, no longer felt like something that could be assumed just because other people said so.

Over time these habits became woven into his days. He scanned every room on entering, checked exits, and silently tracked where people were standing. On dates or dinners with friends, he was preoccupied with where he could sit, what objects were within reach, and who had come in behind him. In the jewelry store, where customers sometimes leaned in close over the counter, he felt tense when anyone moved into his space without warning. He had become harder to be around, though not because he was unkind; he was distracted, vigilant, and difficult to settle. Being single had started to feel safer than trying to explain why a casual touch could make him recoil or why the sound of a crying child in public could abruptly empty his mind of everything except the need to get oriented.

What finally brought Ethan to treatment was not one dramatic collapse but a growing recognition that his life had narrowed around these moments. He had recently been helping a customer while a child in the store next door began crying, and before he knew it he was no longer fully in the jewelry shop. He could feel the event around him with disturbing immediacy, his heart racing, his attention snapping to every sharp or heavy object in sight. Afterward he was shaken by how quickly it had happened and by how unreal the present had briefly seemed compared with the force of the memory. He came in wanting relief, though even here he was watchful, choosing the chair that let him see the whole office. What frightened him most was the sense that the past could take over without warning, and what he hoped for, cautiously, was not to erase what happened but to live in the present without having to treat every room as if it might suddenly become a war zone.
